source.title: Silhouette-based Gait Foundation Model
source.authors: Ding-Qiang Ye; Chao Fan; Kartik Narayan; Bing-Zhe Wu; Chengwen Luo; Jianqiang Li; Vishal M. Patel

record.file_problem: The full paper text is present. It includes the paper’s references and supplementary-material references, but no supplementary materials.
record.tranche_reason: The paper measures model-size scaling in video-based gait recognition and reports that larger models can saturate or regress, while a part-aware design and more diverse pretraining data change the results. This refines the scope of scaling claims in a new setting; it does not test language-model cross-entropy scaling or compute-optimal allocation.
record.gate_note: The study reports rank-1 recognition accuracy across gait-model sizes, not held-out cross-entropy loss, fitted power laws, or compute-optimal parameter/token allocations. Rows capture the reported model-size comparisons bearing on scaling and downstream performance. Other benchmark results, healthcare-task results, and ablations not comparing model sizes are not rows for these claim versions.
record.test_reason: The study scales silhouette-based gait-recognition CNNs from 0.006B to 0.13B parameters, a roughly 20x range. It reports downstream rank-1 accuracy, mostly at two sizes in tables. It never measures held-out loss, never fits a power law and never relates performance to pretraining loss. V5 is about the power-law form in other modalities, which accuracy at a few sizes cannot show. V6 concerns downstream predictability of language models, and these are not language models. The results are informative about whether scaling helps in this domain, but they measure a related construct. They are recorded under fits_no_version rather than as a test of any version.
record.authors_conclusion: The paraphrase is essentially correct. The authors claim to show, for the first time, that vision-based gait pretraining can benefit from scaling trends. They say this requires preserving part-level diversity (part-aware encoding) and diverse pretraining data, while naively enlarging existing models saturates or regresses. FoundationGait follows the scaling trend of Fig. 3 up to 0.13B (20x); scaling to 1B is left as future work.
record.recipe_differences: This study scales video-based gait-recognition models and evaluates rank-1 accuracy; it does not use the original language-model cross-entropy scaling procedure or fit parameter/token/compute loss laws.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported scaling outcome changes with model design (part-aware versus standard), pretraining corpus (GaitLU-1M versus WebGait-2M), and evaluation dataset. The paper also reports that WebGait-2M’s greater diversity matters at matched data scale.

fits_no_version.finding: In video gait recognition, enlarging existing models (self-supervised GaitSSB, supervised DeepGaitV2) from about 0.006B to 0.13B parameters makes rank-1 accuracy saturate or fall. Examples: GaitSSB on GaitLU-1M drops 10.9% on OU-MVLP; DeepGaitV2 on Gait3D drops from 73.3 to 70.8. A part-aware design gives mostly monotonic gains, e.g. FoundationGait Gait3D rank-1 rises from 41.1 to 48.0.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In non-text vision domains, downstream accuracy gains from model size depend on architecture and pretraining data diversity. Naive scaling can saturate or regress.

fits_no_version.finding: At a matched 1M-sequence pretraining scale, the more diverse WebGait-1M beats GaitLU-1M for 0.13B models. The gain is 6.6% on average for GaitSSB and 19.5% for FoundationGait (Table 7a).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Data diversity, not only data quantity, governs whether larger models benefit from pretraining.

record.problems: The scaling comparisons use rank-1 accuracy rather than held-out loss and cover a limited model-size range up to 0.13B; the paper reports no fitted power-law exponents, uncertainty estimates, or compute-optimal allocation analysis. Several scaling figures are described in text, but the tabulated comparisons cover only selected sizes.
record.rows_left_out: Left out the remaining Table 3 dataset/metric comparisons and other benchmark results that do not add a distinct scaling outcome to the retained model-size comparisons; also left out healthcare and unrelated task evaluations. Relevant scaling tables are Tables 3 and 6(b), with broader scaling discussion in Sections 3.1 and 4.3.

untested.parts: Held-out language-model loss versus parameters, tokens or compute; power-law fits.
Extrapolating fitted laws from small runs to much larger runs.
Loss at fixed parameter count across shapes.
Power-law form of loss in a non-text modality. Only downstream accuracy at 2 to 4 sizes is reported, with no fit.
Downstream predictability for language models, from scale or from pretraining loss.
Dependence of exponents and allocation on setup and fitting choices.

missing.what: GaitSSB scaled from 0.006B to 0.13B on GaitLU-1M: CASIA-B NM -7.7, BG -10.8, OU-MVLP -10.9, SUSTech1K -9.0. Neither model benefits from GaitLU-1M.
Multi-size scaling curves for 0.006B, 0.01B, 0.03B and 0.13B on Gait3D and CCPG (GaitSSB vs FoundationGait), and DeepGaitV2 with and without part-aware training.
Fine-tuning results comparing 0.03B and 0.13B: FoundationGait gains on CCPG, CCGR-MINI and Gait3D. On healthcare tasks the 0.13B model is sometimes worse, e.g. Scoliosis1K F1 85.1 vs 91.7.
DroneGait unseen-domain results: GaitSSB-0.13B is below its 0.03B version on mid-pitch views, while FoundationGait improves with size.
Effect of pretraining diversity at matched 1M scale.

record.verdict_notes: A gait-recognition foundation-model paper. 'Scaling trends' here means accuracy rising with model size; it involves no loss, no power-law fits and no compute accounting. The reader's V5/V6 links and labels are dropped. Rows r13 to r15 were mislabelled 'partial' when the larger model is actually worse. The comparisons also confound size with design: the 0.13B FoundationGait was trained for 80K iterations with a cosine schedule, while the other sizes used 40K with step decay.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out language-model pretraining loss as a function of parameters, tokens, or compute; bottleneck conditions and power-law fits.
Whether power laws fitted on small runs predict much larger runs.
Compute-optimal parameter/token allocations and their trends with compute.
Loss comparisons at fixed parameter count across depth, width, and other architecture details.

The study tests model-size scaling in video gait recognition using rank-1 accuracy, but does not fit or establish a power-law form, measure held-out loss, span several orders of magnitude in model size, or test image, repeated-data, fine-tuning, and transfer scaling laws generally.
The study reports downstream gait-recognition results across model sizes, but does not test prediction from pretraining loss or fit a predictive relationship between scale and downstream performance.
Fitted exponents, compute-optimal splits, parameter-counting or fitting choices, and whether fitted loss curves bend away from power laws.

rows.note: The model-size comparison shows higher downstream accuracy at 0.13B.
rows.check: FoundationGait OU-MVLP rank-1 rises from 57.0 to 64.5 (0.03B to 0.13B). This is downstream accuracy of a gait CNN at two sizes; it cannot show a power-law form (V5) and is not a language model (V6).

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.reason: Model-size effects are method- and dataset-dependent: FoundationGait improves on the reported WebGait-2M comparisons, while GaitSSB and supervised DeepGaitV2 include regressions; the study does not establish a common power-law form (r1–r16).

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: FoundationGait self-supervised on WebGait-2M, OU-MVLP and Gait3D
reader_labels.reason: The larger FoundationGait checkpoint has higher rank-1 accuracy than the 0.03B checkpoint on both listed datasets (r1–r2).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.reason: Larger checkpoints do not consistently improve downstream rank-1 performance: several comparisons are lower, and results differ by model design and dataset (r5–r16).
